front.title: Cross-Domain ID Token Hint for OAuth 2.0 Pushed Authorization Requests

abstract.t: This specification defines a mechanism for including an ID Token from an external Identity Provider as a hint in OAuth 2.0 Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR). This enables scenarios where a client (such as an AI agent) needs to prove user identity to an Authorization Server in a different trust domain, while maintaining cryptographic binding between the user identity and the requesting client.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: In modern distributed systems, particularly those involving autonomous AI agents, there is a need for clients to prove user identity to Authorization Servers that are external to the user's home Identity Provider. Traditional OAuth 2.0 flows assume the Authorization Server and Identity Provider share a trust relationship, but cross-domain scenarios require additional mechanisms.
This specification extends the use of id_token_hint parameter in Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR) to support cross-domain identity assertions. It defines:

ul.li: How to include an externally-issued ID Token in a PAR request;
Security requirements for Authorization Server validation;
Mandatory audience binding to prevent token misuse;
Freshness and replay prevention requirements;
Integration with OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication [I-D.ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth], which Authorization Servers MUST support for AI agent authorization scenarios.

section.t: A key use case is AI agent authorization: an agent operating on behalf of a user needs to access resources at a third-party service. The agent can present the user's ID Token (issued by the user's Identity Provider) to the third-party's Authorization Server, proving that the agent is authorized to act for that user.

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.title: Applicability
section.t: While this specification is optimized for use with Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR) , the mechanism defined herein is designed to be general-purpose and MAY be used with various OAuth 2.0 authorization flows, including but not limited to:

ul.li: Authorization Code Grant (with or without PAR);
Client Credentials Grant;
Token Exchange ;
Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant.

section.t: Different authorization flows may have different security considerations when using this specification. Implementations SHOULD carefully evaluate the security implications based on their specific deployment scenario.

section.title: Terminology
section.t: This specification uses the following terms:

dl.dd: The OpenID Provider that authenticates the user and issues ID Tokens. This is typically the user's primary identity service.
An OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server in a different trust domain from the Home IdP. The External AS needs to verify the user's identity before granting access.

The OAuth 2.0 client requesting authorization. In the AI agent context, the client is authenticated using a workload identity through OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication or OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication .
An ID Token issued by the Home IdP, presented to an External AS as proof of user identity.

section.title: Protocol Flow
section.t: The cross-domain ID Token hint flow operates as follows:
The steps are:

ol.li: The user authenticates with their Home IdP through the client (agent).
The Home IdP issues an ID Token with the client's identifier in the aud claim, binding the token to that specific client.

The client sends a PAR request to the External AS, including the ID Token as id_token_hint and authenticating using its client credentials (via OAuth-Client-Attestation and OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP headers).
The External AS validates the ID Token, verifies the audience binding, and confirms the client authentication matches.
The AS returns a request_uri for the authorization flow.
If additional user consent is required, the authorization flow proceeds. If the ID Token is sufficient (consent-only flow), this step may be skipped.
The AS issues a token following standard OAuth 2.0 procedures. Subsequent token usage is out of scope of this specification.

section.title: PAR Request with Cross-Domain ID Token Hint
Request Parameters
section.t: When using a cross-domain ID Token hint, the PAR request MUST include the following parameters:

dl.dd: REQUIRED. The ID Token issued by the Home IdP. This token MUST be a valid JWT signed by the Home IdP.

REQUIRED. The client identifier at the External AS. When using OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication [I-D.ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth] or OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication [I-D.ietf-oauth-spiffe-client-auth], this identifier MUST be derived from the attestation token's (WIT or SVID) sub claim, which typically contains a SPIFFE ID that uniquely identifies the workload.
OPTIONAL. The issuer identifier of the Home IdP. If not provided, the AS MUST extract this from the iss claim of the ID Token.

section.section:
The following is an example PAR request using a cross-domain ID Token hint with OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication:
POST /par HTTP/1.1 Host: as.external-service.example Content-Type: application/oauth-authz-req+jwt OAuth-Client-Attestation: eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IndpdCtqd3QifQ.ewogICJpc3MiOiAic3BpZmZlOi8vZXhhbXBsZS5jb20iLAogICJzdWIiOiAic3BpZmZlOi8vbXlhc3Npc3RhbnQuZXhhbXBsZS9hZ2VudCIsCiAgImF1ZCI6ICJodHRwczovL2FzLmV4dGVybmFsLXNlcnZpY2UuZXhhbXBsZSIsCiAgImV4cCI6IDE3MzEzNjk1NDAsCiAgImNuZiI6IHsiandrIjogeyJrdHkiOiJFQyIsImNydiI6IlAtMjU2IiwieCI6Ii4uLiIsInkiOiIuLi4ifX19.signature OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP: eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6Im9hdXRoLWNsaWVudC1hdHRlc3RhdGlvbi1wb3Arand0In0.ewogICJpc3MiOiAic3BpZmZlOi8vbXlhc3Npc3RhbnQuZXhhbXBsZS9hZ2VudCIsCiAgImF1ZCI6ICJodHRwczovL2FzLmV4dGVybmFsLXNlcnZpY2UuZXhhbXBsZSIsCiAgImlhdCI6IDE3MzEzMjA0MDAsCiAgImV4cCI6IDE3MzEzMjQwMDB9.pop_signature
client_id=spiffe://myassistant.example/agent &id_token_hint=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9... &redirect_uri=https://myassistant.example/callback
The OAuth-Client-Attestation header contains a WIT-SVID with:
typ: wit+jwt: Identifies this as a Workload Identity Token;
sub: The SPIFFE ID of the client (spiffe://myassistant.example/agent);
cnf: Contains the public key that will be used for proof-of-possession;
attestation: (Optional) Embedded attestation evidence from the workload environment.
The OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP header contains a JWT signed with the private key corresponding to the public key in the WIT's cnf claim, demonstrating that the client holds the key.
The id_token_hint contains an ID Token issued by the Agent's Identity Provider (IdP). This ID Token serves two purposes:
Prove Agent Legitimacy: The AS verifies that the requesting agent is legitimate and has authenticated the user;
Assert Third-Party Binding: The ID Token MAY include an extension claim asserting the user's identity at a third-party Resource Application, obtained through on-demand OAuth login.
The aud claim contains the agent's identifier (from the WIT's sub claim), binding this ID Token to the specific agent. The sub claim contains the user's identifier at the Agent's IdP. For cross-domain scenarios involving third-party applications, the ID Token SHOULD include a third_party_binding claim conveying the user's identity at the Resource Application.
WIT-SVID's sub claim), binding this ID Token to the specific agent:
{ "iss": "https://idp.agent-a.example", "sub": "agent_user_001", "aud": "spiffe://agent-a.example", "exp": 1731369540, "iat": 1731320400, "nonce": "n-0S6_WzA2Mj", "auth_time": 1731320380,
"third_party_binding": { "app": "shop.example", "user_id": "user_12345", "bound_at": 1731320400, "oauth_flow_completed": true } }
In the lazy binding scenario (recommended for AI agent workflows), the user does not pre-register with all possible third-party applications. Instead, when the agent detects intent to invoke a specific third-party application during conversation, it triggers an on-demand OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow with that application. Upon successful user authentication, the third-party application issues an ID Token containing the user's identifier (e.g., user_12345). The Agent's IdP then asserts this binding in the third_party_binding claim, enabling the AS to issue an access token with the correct Resource Application user identifier.

section.title: Authorization Server Validation
section.t: Upon receiving a PAR request with a cross-domain ID Token hint, the Authorization Server MUST perform the following validation steps:

section.title: Client Authentication Validation
section.t: The Authorization Server MUST support OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication for AI agent authorization scenarios. This specification requires the use of attestation-based client authentication to ensure strong cryptographic binding between the client identity and the user identity conveyed in the id_token_hint.
Before validating the ID Token hint, the AS MUST first authenticate the client using OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication or OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication .
The AS MUST validate the client authentication as follows:

li.t: Accept Valid Header Types: The AS MUST accept wit+jwt as a valid value of the typ JWT header parameter in the OAuth-Client-Attestation header, in addition to oauth-client-attestation-jwt.
Validate WIT/WIT-SVID: The WIT or WIT-SVID MUST be validated according to Section 3.1 of or the equivalent validation rules in . This includes:

ul.li: Verifying the JWT signature using the trust domain's public keys;
Verifying that the WIT has not expired (check the exp claim);
Extracting the client identifier from the sub claim.

li.t: Validate Proof-of-Possession: The OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP JWT MUST be validated according to Section 5.2 of . The AS MUST verify that the PoP JWT is signed with the private key corresponding to the public key bound in the WIT's cnf claim.

section.t: After successful client authentication, the AS extracts the client identifier from the WIT's sub claim and uses it for audience binding validation with the id_token_hint.

section.title: ID Token Signature Validation
section.t: The AS MUST validate the ID Token signature using the public keys of the Home IdP. The AS MUST obtain these keys through one of the following methods:

ul.li: Pre-configured trust: The AS has a pre-established trust relationship with the Home IdP and has access to its signing keys.
OpenID Discovery: The AS fetches the IdP's metadata from /.well-known/openid-configuration and retrieves the JWKS.
Federation: The AS participates in an identity federation that includes the Home IdP.

section.t: If the AS cannot validate the ID Token signature, it MUST reject the request with an invalid_request error.

section.title: Audience Binding Validation
section.t: The AS MUST verify that the ID Token's aud claim matches the authenticated client identity. This binding ensures that the ID Token was issued specifically for the requesting client.
The validation rule is:

When using OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication or OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication, the client_id is derived from the WIT's or SVID's sub claim. The AS MUST perform the following validation sequence:

ol.li: First, cryptographically verify the WIT/SVID signature using the trusted issuer's public key. The WIT/SVID MUST be valid and not expired.
Only after signature verification succeeds, extract the sub claim from the WIT/SVID.
Verify that the ID Token's aud claim matches the WIT/SVID's sub claim:

section.t: This sequence ensures that the audience binding comparison is only performed against a cryptographically verified client identity.
If the audience does not match, the AS MUST reject the request with an invalid_request error and the following error description:
This audience binding is critical for security. It prevents an attacker from obtaining a user's ID Token intended for one client and presenting it to an AS while impersonating a different client.

section.title: Freshness Validation
section.t: The AS MUST verify that the ID Token is fresh and has not expired:

ul.li: The exp claim MUST be in the future.
The AS MAY enforce a maximum age for the ID Token (e.g., the token MUST have been issued within the last 5 minutes for high-security operations).
If the AS requires a specific nonce, it MUST verify the nonce value matches the expected value.

section.title: Replay Prevention
section.t: To prevent replay attacks, the AS SHOULD implement one or more of the following mechanisms:

ul.li: Nonce validation: Require a nonce claim in the ID Token that matches a value previously communicated to the client.
One-time use: Track used ID Tokens by their jti claim (if present) and reject duplicates.
Short expiry: Enforce a short maximum age for ID Tokens used as hints (e.g., 5 minutes).

DPoP binding: If the client uses DPoP for the PAR request, the AS MAY require the ID Token to contain a cnf claim binding it to the same public key used in the DPoP proof. Note that this requires the Home IdP to support key-bound ID Tokens.

section.title: Access Token Issuance
section.t: Upon successful validation of the id_token_hint, the AS issues an Access Token. The Access Token structure follows OAuth 2.0 standards with specific considerations for cross-domain AI agent scenarios.

section.title: Subject (sub) Claim
section.t: The sub claim in the Access Token MUST contain the user's identifier at the Resource Application (third-party app), NOT the Agent's internal user identifier. This design enables the Resource Server to immediately identify the resource owner without additional identity mapping lookups.

For example, if the user authenticated with shop.example and obtained the identifier user_12345, the Access Token's sub claim MUST be user_12345, even though the Agent's IdP issued the id_token_hint with a different identifier (agent_user_001).

The AS extracts the Resource Application user identifier from the third_party_binding.user_id claim in the id_token_hint and uses it as the sub claim value in the Access Token. This is based on trust in the Agent's IdP, which has verified the OAuth login flow with the Resource Application.

section.title: Actor (act) Claim
section.t: The AS SHOULD include the act claim as defined in to indicate that the client is acting on behalf of the user. The act claim contains:

ul.li: sub: The Agent's WIT URI, identifying the entity exercising delegated authority;
agent_user_id (OPTIONAL): The user's identifier at the Agent system, enabling audit trail correlation at the Agent side.

section.t: In this example:

ul.li: sub: "user_12345": The user's identifier at shop.example (the Resource Application). This is what the Resource Server uses to identify the resource owner.
act.sub: "wit://agent-a.example": The Agent's WIT URI, identifying which agent is exercising delegated authority.
act.agent_user_id: "agent_user_001": Optional field for Agent-side audit purposes, allowing correlation back to the Agent's internal user account.

section.title: Comparison with Token Exchange
section.t: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange provides another mechanism for cross-domain token operations. This section clarifies when to use each approach.

section.title: Token Exchange (RFC 8693)
section.t: Token Exchange is designed for scenarios where a token needs to be exchanged for another token, typically with different scope, audience, or token type. Common use cases include:

ul.li: Service-to-service delegation chains where each hop requires a new token;
Impersonation scenarios where an administrator acts as another user;
Converting token types (e.g., access token to refresh token).

section.t: Token Exchange requires implementing a dedicated token exchange endpoint and supporting the urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange grant type.

section.title: Cross-Domain ID Token Hint (This Specification)
section.t: This specification addresses a different use case: proving user identity across trust domains during the authorization request phase. Key characteristics include:

ul.li: The ID Token serves as a hint, not as input for token exchange;
Integrates with existing PAR infrastructure without new endpoints;
Audience binding ensures the token was issued specifically for this client;
Lower implementation complexity for Authorization Servers.

section.title: Recommended Usage
section.t: Use this specification when:

ul.li: An AI agent needs to prove it represents a specific user to an external service;
The goal is to obtain authorization, not to exchange existing tokens;
Client identity binding (via audience) is a security requirement.

section.t: Use Token Exchange when:

ul.li: An existing token needs to be converted to a different token type;
Backend services need to propagate delegated authority through multiple hops;
Impersonation or delegation semantics are explicitly required.

section.title: Trust Establishment
section.t: The External AS must establish trust in the Home IdP before accepting ID Tokens. This trust can be established through:

ul.li: Pre-configured trust relationships;
Federation membership;
Dynamic trust establishment with appropriate verification.

section.t: The AS MUST NOT accept ID Tokens from untrusted issuers.

section.title: Audience Binding Security
section.t: The audience binding requirement () is essential for preventing token substitution attacks. Without this binding, an attacker could:

ol.li: Obtain a user's ID Token issued to a legitimate client;
Present the token while authenticating as a different (malicious) client;
Gain unauthorized access on behalf of the user.

section.t: The audience binding ensures that only the intended client can use the ID Token.

section.title: ID Token Confidentiality
section.t: ID Tokens used as hints contain user identity information and MUST be protected in transit. The PAR endpoint MUST be accessed over TLS.
Clients SHOULD treat ID Tokens as sensitive credentials and MUST NOT log or store them unnecessarily.

section.title: Token Lifetime
section.t: ID Tokens used for cross-domain hints SHOULD have short lifetimes to minimize the window for replay attacks. The AS MAY reject ID Tokens that are older than a configured threshold, even if they have not technically expired.

section.title: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Cross-domain ID Token hints involve sharing user identity information between trust domains. Implementations MUST consider:

ul.li: User consent: The user should be aware that their identity is being shared with an external service.
Minimal disclosure: The ID Token should contain only the claims necessary for the authorization decision.
Pairwise identifiers: Where possible, use pairwise subject identifiers to prevent correlation across services.

section.title: Relationship to OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication
section.t: This specification relies on OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication and OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication for client authentication. These specifications work together:

ul.li: OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication: Defines the general framework for using attestation tokens as OAuth client credentials, including the HTTP header format (OAuth-Client-Attestation and OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP).
OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication: Specializes the attestation-based authentication for SPIFFE environments, defining how to use JWT-SVID or WIT-SVID as client credentials.
WIMSE Workload Credentials : Defines the structure of Workload Identity Tokens (WIT) and Workload Proof Tokens (WPT), which can be used within the OAuth attestation framework.
Cross-Domain ID Token Hint: Conveys the user's identity from an external Identity Provider, bound to the client identity established through attestation-based authentication.

section.t: Together, these specifications enable a complete solution for AI agent authorization where the agent proves both its own identity (using attestation-backed workload credentials) and the user's identity to an external Authorization Server.
